content: In anatomy, the term areola (plural: areolae), derived from the Latin word area meaning open place, refers to any small circular area. Most commonly, it describes the pigmented skin surrounding the human nipple, known as the areola mammae. However, the term can also apply to other small circular regions, such as the inflamed area around a pimple. The Merriam-Webster dictionary provides two pronunciations for areola: a-REE-o-la and a-re-O-la, with audio examples available for clarity. The distinct coloration of the areola compared to the rest of the breast is due to its anatomical association with the ducts of the mammary glands. Upon close examination of a mature female nipple, one can observe several small openings arranged radially around the nipple's tip. These are the lactiferous ducts, which release milk during lactation. Additionally, the areola contains sebaceous glands called Montgomery's glands (or glands of Montgomery). These glands secrete lubricating substances to protect the nipple area and facilitate suckling during breastfeeding. These glands may appear raised above the areola's surface, giving a goose-flesh appearance. The pigmentation of the areola is influenced by two polymers: brown eumelanin and red pheomelanin. The relative proportions of these pigments determine the areola's color, which can range from pale pink to dark brown. Generally, individuals with lighter skin tones tend to have paler areolae, while those with darker skin tones have darker areolae. Hormonal changes, such as those caused by menstruation, certain medications, or aging, can also alter the color of the areolae over time. Notably, during pregnancy, the areolae often darken significantly. After childbirth, some degree of color regression may occur, but this varies between individuals. The size and shape of areolae are highly variable. In sexually mature women, areolae are typically larger than those of men or prepubescent girls. While most human areolae are circular, some women and men have noticeably elliptical areolae. The average diameter of male areolae is approximately 25 mm (1 inch), whereas sexually mature women may have areolae ranging up to 100 mm (4 inches) or more in diameter, with an average size of around 30 mm (1 3/8 inches). Women who are lactating or have particularly large breasts may have even larger areolae.
